432.text:
Yachts, designer handbags and sports cars are bought by only a few, and some argue that higher taxes on luxury goods reduce inequality. I agree only to a limited extent, since such taxes raise some money from the wealthy, but wealth is better addressed through income and property taxes.

To begin with, luxury taxes can make a small contribution. They raise some revenue from wealthy buyers and make the tax system look fairer. A tax of twenty per cent on a yacht, for example, falls almost entirely on people who have plenty of money and who can afford to pay it, and the proceeds can fund schools or healthcare that benefit poorer people. Because luxury goods are not necessities, taxing them does not harm the poor. Higher prices may also discourage showy consumption, which can reduce the social pressure that people feel to compete in spending. Several countries have used such taxes on cars, jewellery and watches.

However, the amounts are small, buyers can purchase abroad and jobs in luxury industries may suffer. The wealthiest people can buy a yacht in another country or register it elsewhere, and the revenue from luxury items is tiny compared with income tax or property tax. Factories that produce fine furniture or jewellery may lose orders and dismiss craft workers. Broader progressive taxation is more effective. Higher rates of income tax for top earners, taxes on inheritance and capital gains, and a modest annual tax on very large fortunes raise far more money, while spending on education, health care and housing for poorer families addresses inequality directly.

In conclusion, higher taxes on luxury goods reduce inequality only to a limited extent, and governments should rely mainly on wider progressive taxation.

434.text:
Cocoa, coffee, cotton and many other goods are produced by farmers and workers who earn very little, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for ensuring fair trade or whether society and government should enforce it. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that shoppers can promote fair trade through their choices. Consumers can choose certified goods and press companies for better practice. A customer who consistently buys fair-trade coffee, for example, increases demand for it and encourages shops to stock more, while collective boycotts and social media campaigns have forced several companies to improve conditions. Consumers who ask where products come from send a signal to businesses that ethics matter, and companies depend on their customers. Many people feel that moral duty begins with their own spending, and personal action does not need to wait for legislation.

On the other hand, advocates of government enforcement point out that supply chains are too complex for individuals to check. Shoppers cannot visit factories, and labels can be misleading. A person who buys a shirt that passes through several countries cannot know whether any worker was underpaid. Governments must therefore require transparency and punish exploitation. Laws can oblige companies to investigate their suppliers, ban goods made with forced labour and set minimum standards, while labour inspectors and international agreements enforce them. Fair trade needs informed consumers and enforceable laws. Without legal rules, firms that behave ethically may lose business to cheaper rivals who do not.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility is shared: individuals should buy ethically where they can, but governments must set and enforce rules that apply to all companies.

440.text:
Some shoppers walk to a farmers' market for tomatoes grown ten kilometres away, while others buy mangoes flown across the world, and opinions differ on whether it is better to buy local produce or imported goods. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of local produce argue that it is fresher and supports farmers. Food grown nearby needs less transport and keeps money in the region. A family that buys vegetables from a farmer in the next village, for example, enjoys produce that was picked yesterday and helps to sustain local jobs. Short journeys mean lower emissions and less packaging, and consumers can learn how their food was grown. Local farms also preserve countryside and traditional varieties, and buying in season encourages a healthy variety of diets. In an emergency, a country with strong local agriculture is less dependent on foreign supply.

On the other hand, supporters of imported goods argue that they offer variety and lower prices. Imported goods supply out-of-season and exotic items often at a lower cost. A shopper in a cold country, for example, can eat fresh fruit in winter and enjoy tea, spices and coffee that cannot grow locally. Specialisation means that some regions can produce food much more efficiently, so that imported produce may even have a smaller carbon footprint than local greenhouse crops. Trade also provides income for farmers in developing countries. However, long supply chains can hide poor labour conditions, and the freshness of imports may be lower. A mix of both suits most households.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that people should buy local produce in season when possible, but they can also enjoy imported goods that cannot be grown nearby.

444.text:
Large companies often pay little tax even when they make huge profits, and this essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take to reduce corporate tax avoidance, focusing on closing loopholes and on international cooperation.

To begin with, governments can reduce tax avoidance by closing loopholes. Firms shift profits to low-tax countries through transfer pricing and shell companies, so reporting rules, a minimum rate and penalties limit it. A technology firm that books its profits in a small country where it has few staff, for example, can pay a rate far lower than a local shop. Countries can require companies to publish how much revenue, profit and tax they declare in every country, which makes artificial arrangements visible. Rules can also limit deductions for interest and royalties paid to related companies, and tax on profits can be linked to where sales and employees actually are. Strong penalties and well-trained auditors discourage cheating.

In addition, authorities must cooperate internationally. A single country that acts alone risks losing investment, so agreements are needed. A global minimum tax rate, which many countries have now accepted, removes the reward for moving profits to low-tax places. Countries can share information automatically about foreign accounts and companies, and help each other to collect unpaid tax. Public pressure also matters, since consumers and investors may avoid firms with a reputation for avoiding tax. Fairer revenue funds public services and reduces the burden on ordinary taxpayers, who currently pay more than their share.

In conclusion, closing loopholes together with international cooperation offers the most realistic way to reduce corporate tax avoidance.

462.text:
Sales of electric cars are growing, but they still cost more than petrol models, and the question is to what extent governments should subsidise their purchase. I believe that governments should do so to a moderate extent, with subsidies that are temporary and aimed at those who need them.

To begin with, subsidies speed up the shift to cleaner transport. Buyers face high prices and a lack of chargers, so support increases adoption and cuts emissions. A family on a modest income, for example, may only buy an electric car if a grant reduces the price, and each additional electric car replaces a polluting one. As more cars are sold, factories can produce at a larger scale and batteries become cheaper, which eventually removes the need for help. Transport is a major source of greenhouse gases and city air pollution, so early adoption brings benefits to public health as well as to the climate. Subsidies also encourage manufacturers and investors to build charging networks.

However, unlimited subsidies have drawbacks. Grants mostly benefit wealthy households that would have bought an electric car anyway, and they cost public money that could improve public transport, which helps everyone, including people without cars. Support should therefore be time-limited, based on income and linked to investment in charging points, and it should decrease as prices fall. Some countries have already ended or reduced grants once sales were established. Governments may also need to ensure that electricity is produced from clean sources, otherwise the environmental benefit will be limited. Subsidies for used electric cars could help poorer buyers as well.

In conclusion, governments should subsidise electric vehicle purchases to a moderate extent, but only in a temporary, targeted way that is combined with charging infrastructure.

480.text:
Some people hunt through charity shops, online marketplaces and car boot sales, while others prefer the smell and guarantee of something new, and opinions differ on whether it is better to buy second-hand goods or new items. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of second-hand goods argue that they save money and resources. Buying used items cuts waste and cost and can give unique finds. A student who furnishes a flat with second-hand tables and chairs, for example, spends a fraction of the price of new furniture and may find sturdy pieces that are better made than modern ones. Reusing goods reduces the energy and raw materials needed for production and keeps items out of landfill, which helps the environment. Vintage clothing and old books can be unique, and selling used items gives sellers some money back. Children's clothes and toys are used for such a short time that buying new ones often seems wasteful.

On the other hand, supporters of new goods argue that they offer reliability and a warranty. New products are cleaner, come with guarantees and may last longer for essential items. A person who buys a used fridge, for example, may find that it breaks down within months or uses a lot of electricity, while a new model has a warranty and is energy-efficient. For items such as mattresses, helmets and electronic devices, safety, hygiene and up-to-date technology matter. New goods also match exactly what the buyer wants. The choice depends on the item and budget. For furniture, clothes and books, second-hand is often sensible, but for safety equipment and key appliances, new may be better.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that buying second-hand is a smart habit where quality and safety are not at risk.

484.text:
When recessions arrive, theatres, design studios, publishers and film crews often lose customers first, and this essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take to support creative industries during economic downturns, focusing on emergency finance and on helping the sector to adapt.

To begin with, governments can protect creative industries with emergency funds, tax relief and commissions. Artists and studios rely on irregular income and discretionary spending, so grants, loans, public contracts and help with digital and foreign markets keep talent and skills alive. A theatre company that cannot sell tickets during a crisis, for example, can survive with a government grant that pays rent and wages until audiences return. Temporary reductions in sales tax and business charges leave more money in the sector, while loans on favourable terms prevent firms from collapsing. Governments can also commission murals, films, music and design for public buildings and campaigns, which gives work to many freelancers.

In addition, authorities should help the sector to adapt and to grow. Training in digital skills allows creators to sell online, and export agencies can help studios to reach foreign markets where demand may be stronger. Shared workspaces at low rent and funds for new ideas encourage start-ups, and income support for self-employed artists prevents them from leaving the profession. Equally important, protecting copyright ensures that creators are paid when their work is used. The sector recovers faster and contributes to growth, since creative industries employ many people and attract tourists, and a recession is a time to preserve skills that would take years to rebuild.

In conclusion, emergency finance together with support for adaptation and export offers the most realistic way to protect creative industries in a downturn.

485.text:
On a Saturday morning, stalls piled with heirloom tomatoes, unusual beans and rare fruits attract crowds in many towns, and this essay will discuss the role of local markets in preserving food diversity, focusing on traditional varieties and on small farmers.

To begin with, local markets preserve food diversity by giving small farmers a place to sell traditional varieties. Supermarkets favour a few uniform, long-lasting products, whereas market stalls sell local, seasonal and rare crops. A farmer who grows an old variety of apple that is sweet but bruises easily, for example, cannot supply a supermarket chain, but she can sell it at a market where customers appreciate its taste. Without this outlet, such crops would disappear because there would be no reason to grow them. Seeds that are passed from one generation to the next carry genetic variety that is valuable for resisting disease and climate change. Markets also let shoppers taste, ask questions and discover unfamiliar products.

Furthermore, markets keep recipes and culture alive. Cooks learn from sellers how to prepare unusual vegetables, and traditional dishes depend on local ingredients that supermarkets do not stock. Direct sales give farmers a fairer share of the price, which helps them to stay on the land and to keep growing diverse crops. However, markets face competition from supermarkets and rising rents, and some sell the same imported goods as shops. Support for markets protects biodiversity and culture. Councils can offer cheap stall space, protect market sites in city centres and promote events that highlight local produce, while schools can teach children about traditional foods.

In conclusion, local markets play an important role in preserving food diversity by supporting small farmers and traditional crops, and they deserve public support.

490.text:
Cars, food, medicines and electronics are recalled because of defects almost every week, and many people say that quality control in manufacturing is insufficient. I agree to some extent, since cost-cutting and long supply chains often outweigh inspection, although leading firms invest heavily in testing.

To begin with, quality control is insufficient where cost-cutting and long supply chains outweigh inspection. Recalls of cars, food and electronics show that defects pass checks when companies rush or outsource. A carmaker that discovers a faulty airbag only after millions of vehicles have been sold, for example, shows that its testing did not detect a problem that affected safety and cost lives. Parts are often made by dozens of suppliers in several countries, and a company may not know how each one is produced. Pressure to cut prices and to launch products quickly encourages shortcuts, and inspectors who are few in number cannot check every batch. Cheap goods sold online sometimes bypass inspection altogether.

However, many leading firms invest heavily in testing, and quality has improved in many industries. Automated cameras and sensors inspect products at high speed, and statistical methods identify problems early. A modern electronics factory, for example, may test every component and run each device through hours of stress tests before it leaves the line. Strict standards in aircraft and medicine are enforced and have produced very low failure rates. Inspection must be independent and continuous. Governments should require traceability of parts, fund independent testing, impose heavy penalties for hiding defects and protect employees who report problems, while companies should treat quality as a priority and not as a cost.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that quality control in manufacturing is insufficient, particularly where cost pressure is strong, but good systems exist and can be spread more widely.
